blocks.text: Hallucination reduction covers the broader set of strategies for minimizing fabricated, unsupported claims in a model response, building directly on the grounding techniques covered in the previous topic while adding uncertainty acknowledgment, explicit refusal behavior, sampling settings, and cross-referencing multiple sources.

This topic covers why hallucination happens as a natural consequence of how a model generates text, the full toolkit of mitigation levers beyond grounding alone, and the important reality that these techniques reduce, but do not fully eliminate, hallucination.
1. What Hallucination Actually Is

blocks.alt: Building on grounding techniques, hallucination reduction covers multiple mitigation levers

blocks.text: Hallucination refers to a model generating a confident sounding claim that is actually false or entirely unsupported, whether by its own training knowledge or by any retrieved context provided to it, this is a genuine, well documented behavior worth actively designing against.

blocks.alt: Confident sounding output can still contain a fabricated claim with no real basis

blocks.text: 2. Why Hallucination Happens

blocks.alt: The model predicts the most probable next token with no built in fact verification step

blocks.text: This connects directly back to the earlier How LLMs Process Prompts topic, a model generates text by predicting the most probable next token given everything before it, it has no separate, built in fact-checking mechanism verifying that a generated claim is actually true, a fluent, plausible sounding continuation can be generated with equal confidence whether it is accurate or not.
3. Grounding as the Primary Lever

blocks.alt: Grounding techniques are the primary lever, alongside uncertainty acknowledgment and explicit refusal

blocks.text: The grounding techniques covered in the previous topic, required quotes, self-verification, structured extraction, remain the single most effective lever for reducing hallucination in a RAG context specifically, since they tie claims directly to verifiable source material rather than the model unconstrained generation.
4. Instructing the Model to Acknowledge Uncertainty

blocks.alt: No instruction to express uncertainty is compared against an explicit instruction to express uncertainty

blocks.text: A model given no explicit permission to express uncertainty tends to default toward a confident sounding answer even when the underlying information is genuinely thin, explicitly instructing the model to state its uncertainty when the evidence is incomplete or ambiguous directly counters this default.

code.content:
prompt = (
    "If the context only partially answers the question, or if you are "
    "not confident in part of your answer, explicitly say so rather than "
    "presenting an uncertain claim with full confidence."
)

blocks.text: 5. Instructing Explicit Refusal When Genuinely Unsure

Beyond simply expressing uncertainty, some situations warrant an explicit refusal to answer at all, "the provided context does not contain enough information to answer this question," this connects directly to the fallback instruction covered in the earlier Retrieval Prompting topic, a genuinely important tool for high stakes applications where a wrong confident answer is worse than no answer.
6. Sampling Settings and Hallucination

blocks.alt: Higher temperature produces more creative variation, lower temperature produces more conservative, grounded output

blocks.text: A model sampling temperature, covered briefly in an earlier module, controls how much randomness enters the generation process, a lower temperature setting tends to produce more conservative, predictable output that stays closer to the most probable, evidence supported continuation, reducing the model tendency to wander into more creative, less grounded territory.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Setting","Effect on Hallucination Risk"],"rows":[["Higher temperature","More variation, somewhat higher hallucination risk"],["Lower temperature","More conservative output, generally lower risk"]]}

blocks.text: 7. Cross-Referencing Multiple Sources

blocks.alt: A claim from a single source is compared against a claim cross referenced across multiple sources

blocks.text: When retrieval returns more than one relevant source, this connects to multi-document prompting, covered later in this module, instructing the model to note whether a claim is corroborated across multiple sources, or only supported by one, adds another signal for how much confidence a claim actually deserves.

blocks.title: This mirrors basic journalistic and research practice
blocks.content: Corroborating a claim across independent sources before treating it as reliable is a long established practice outside AI as well, applying the same discipline to retrieved source material is a natural extension of that idea.

blocks.text: 8. Hallucination Reduction Is Not Elimination

It is important to be realistic here, these techniques meaningfully reduce hallucination rate, they do not guarantee it never happens, a production system handling anything genuinely high stakes should still pair these prompting techniques with output validation, covered in an earlier module, and human review where appropriate.
9. Measuring Hallucination Rate

This connects directly to the metric-driven iteration process covered in an earlier module, tracking hallucination rate as an explicit metric, checking a sample of responses against their source material for unsupported claims, gives a concrete way to measure whether these mitigation techniques are actually working and by how much.
Worked Example

A team building a medical information retrieval tool finds their assistant occasionally states a specific detail with full confidence that is not actually present in the retrieved medical reference material, a genuinely serious problem for this domain.

Combining grounding techniques from the previous topic, required quotes for every claim, with an explicit instruction to state uncertainty or refuse to answer when the context is incomplete, and lowering the sampling temperature, together reduce this failure rate substantially, measured directly by checking a sample of responses against their source material before and after the changes.
Common Mistakes

items: Relying on only one hallucination reduction technique instead of combining grounding, uncertainty instructions, and sampling settings together
Not giving the model explicit permission to express uncertainty or refuse to answer when evidence is genuinely thin
Assuming these techniques eliminate hallucination entirely rather than meaningfully reducing its rate
Never actually measuring hallucination rate, relying only on a general impression that responses seem accurate

blocks.text: Practice

Take a retrieval prompt you have built or could build, add an explicit uncertainty acknowledgment instruction and a refusal fallback, then test it with a question the context only partially supports, checking whether the model appropriately expresses uncertainty rather than answering with unwarranted confidence.
Key Takeaway

Hallucination happens because a model generates the most probable next text with no built in fact-checking step, and reducing it requires combining several levers together, grounding techniques, explicit uncertainty and refusal instructions, conservative sampling settings, and cross-referencing sources, measured against an actual hallucination rate rather than assumed to be solved.
